                                                         4
Nutrient analysis survey of fresh and processed fruit and vegetables with respect to fibre




Executive summary
This is a survey of the nutrient composition of commonly consumed fruit and
vegetables, with a focus on fibre measured by the Association of Official Analytical
Chemists (AOAC) method. The Carbohydrates and Health report from the Scientific
Advisory Committee on Nutrition (SACN) recommended that dietary fibre should be
defined by this method. There is a need to improve the quality of estimates of fibre
intakes based on the AOAC method, as there is a lack of data on the AOAC fibre
content of foods, particularly fruit and vegetables. This survey provides AOAC fibre
values for a range of fruit and vegetables that have not yet been analysed by this
method and also updates and extends information on other nutrients that were last
analysed in the 1980s. It complements the nutrient analysis of fruit and vegetables
analytical report, 2013 [1], where 59 composite samples were analysed.

The nutrient composition data generated by this survey will be used to update the
National Diet and Nutrition Survey nutrient databank, thus providing more robust data
on nutrient intakes. This update will provide a firm evidence base for the work streams
arising from the SACN Carbohydrates and Health report, which will help to maintain
and improve the evidence base for advice and interventions to reduce premature
deaths and the burden of ill health associated with poor diet. It will also support the
Living Costs and Food Survey and will be disseminated via the authoritative UK food
composition tables, McCance and Widdowson’s The Composition of Foods.

This survey includes analysis of 62 composite samples that were made up of between
6 and 11 sub-samples that were representative of fruit and vegetables consumed in the
UK. Sub-samples included were based on the need to take into account factors
including cultivar, region and country of origin and season. Where necessary, seasonal
sampling was required in order to collect foods from a range of countries. Samples
were purchased from retail outlets and prepared for analysis between July 2015 and
February 2016.

This sampling report gives details of the sub-samples making up each composite
sample. Analytical results from the survey are contained in a separate report. Results
for individual fatty acids are reported separately in electronic format.




                                                         5
Nutrient analysis survey of fresh and processed fruit and vegetables with respect to fibre




Sampling notes
   samples were collected according to a sample protocol produced in agreement with
    Public Health England (PHE)
   sub-samples were agreed with PHE based on a review of market shares and
    nutrient content
   all samples were collected between July 2015 and February 2016 and stored
    according to usual consumer practice or according to packaging guildines until
    required for processing
   where possible all sub-samples within a composite sample were prepared in a single
    day and the composite sample was produced on the same day. Where that was not
    possible, sub-samples were prepared and stored whole and frozen at -20°C until all
    sub-samples were available and the composite sample could be produced. Where
    sub-samples were purchased over several weeks, sub-samples were prepared and
    stored whole and frozen at -40°C until all sub-samples were available. Once all
    season samples had been collected they were partially thawed and homogenised in
    equal proportions to produce the final composite sample
   composite samples were stored at -40°C before being sent to laboratories for
    analysis
   ingredients, label claims and nutrient information presented in this report have been
    taken directly from product packaging

Sample preparation

Purchased samples were stored according to packing guidelines and usual consumer
practices. Ambient products were stored at room temperature and chilled products were
refrigerated at 4°C. Frozen products were stored at -20°C and cooked from frozen,
depending on product guidelines. Details of all sub-samples were recorded prior to
preparation of composite samples and all samples including packaging, ingredient and
nutrition information were photographed.

Where further sample preparation or cooking was required, samples were prepared
according to packaging instructions or based on guidance for consumers provided by a
range of sources including industry trade associations. Equal weights of un-
homogenised sub-samples were combined to form single composite samples. The
composite samples were homogenised as thoroughly as possible and were split into
sub-samples of approximately 100g each. Composite samples were stored at -40°C
before being sent to laboratories for analysis. Where possible all sub-samples within a
composite sample were prepared in a single day and the composite sample could be
produced on the same day. Where that was not possible, sub-samples were prepared
and stored frozen until all sub-samples were available and the composite sample could
be produced. Where samples were purchased over several weeks, sub-samples were
prepared and stored whole and frozen at -40°C until all sub-samples were available.
Once all sub-samples had been collected, they were partially thawed and mixed in
equal proportions to produce the final composite sample for analysis of all nutrients.

Details for each sample are given below, including weight changes on cooking and
edible portion measurements.
